title.title: What's Next for Blockchain?
title.subtitle: Bitcoin is one of the simplest blockchains. Sneak peeks of Ethereum, smart contracts, NFTs, DAOs — and where all of this is heading.

techHint.label: Under the hood →
techHint.title: The deep version lives in Blockchain Platforms, Section 2

ethereum.recapTail: . Vitalik's response: don't patch Bitcoin — build a new chain that can run programs.
ethereum.heading: Ethereum — The Programmable Blockchain
ethereum.lead: Bitcoin is money. Ethereum is a programmable world computer.
ethereum.vitalikBio: Born 1994 in Russia, raised in Canada. Published the Ethereum whitepaper in late 2013 — aged
ethereum.originLine: An early Bitcoin writer, he wanted a blockchain that could run any program — not just move coins.
ethereum.worldBody: One shared computer run by thousands of machines, that anyone can use and nobody owns. Bitcoin stores balances; Ethereum also stores programs — and runs them for anyone who pays the fee.

milestones.label: Launch
milestones.note: Ethereum goes live. Programs on a blockchain, for real.

milestones.label: The Merge → Proof of Stake
milestones.note: Mining replaced by staking. Energy use drops ~99.95%.

milestones.label: The default platform for apps
milestones.note: DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, tokens — most of them started here.

ethAccounts.recapA: Remember — a wallet holds keys, not coins. Ethereum keeps that idea and adds a
ethAccounts.recapTail: of account: one that is run by code instead of a person.
ethAccounts.title: Two Kinds of Account
ethAccounts.intro: Your wallet is a person. A smart contract is a robot that only acts when poked. Everything on Ethereum is one or the other.

eoa.title: Your wallet — a person
points: Whoever holds the key owns the account — that's you
Starts things: send money, poke a contract, publish a new one
Holds a balance and nothing else — there are no rules inside
eoa.examples: your Rabby or Zerion wallet, a hardware wallet, an exchange wallet

contract.title: A smart contract — a robot
points: No key, no owner — the code is the boss
Never moves on its own: it waits until a wallet (or another robot) calls it
Holds its own balance and hands it out exactly as its rules say
contract.examples: Uniswap, the USDC token, an NFT collection

ethAccounts.arrowSub: Every action starts from a wallet — a contract only reacts when called.
ethAccounts.keyRuleBody: Robots never act on their own. Behind every on-chain action there is a key-holder — a human, or a bot a human runs — who pressed the button first.
ethAccounts.peek: You'll deploy a contract account of your own and call it from your wallet.

ethGas.recapBody: A smart contract runs on thousands of computers at once. Somebody pays for that work — that's gas.
ethGas.heading: Gas — Paying the World Computer for Work
ethGas.lead: Every action costs a little gas. Bigger job, more gas. Busier network, higher price per unit. You only pay for what you use.

demo.hint: Drag the sliders, or load a typical operation below.
demo.presetsLabel: Typical gas costs — click to load

rows.note: View call — never hits the chain
Cheap — stored in logs, not state
Base cost for every ETH transfer
Pays for every byte of bytecode

analogy.title: Same maths as filling up a car
analogy.caption: A bigger job burns more units. A busier network raises the price per unit.

surge.title: Busy network = higher fee
surge.body: Like Uber surge pricing: same ride, more people asking, higher price per unit. The gas-price slider is the surge.

ethGas.peek: You'll write a contract and watch the gas meter tick as it runs.

apps.title: DeFi
apps.subtitle: Decentralised Finance
apps.tease: Programmable money, first use: rebuild finance out of smart contracts. Light tour now — a later session goes deep.
apps.description: Lending, trading and earning interest as smart contracts — open 24/7, no account manager, no middleman taking a cut.
apps.risk: Smart contract bugs, oracle manipulation, liquidation cascades
apps.hype: Real and open 24/7 — but most volume is still crypto trading crypto, not everyday finance
apps.later: You'll trace a real token swap through a smart contract, step by step.

visual.orderBookSub: a middleman matches buyers with sellers
visual.orderBookNote: Every trade needs a counterparty and a matchmaker.
visual.ammSub: you trade against a pool, priced by a formula
visual.ammNote: No counterparty needed — the formula sets the price.
visual.bottomLine: DeFi replaces the exchange with a pool + a formula.

apps.title: NFTs
apps.subtitle: Non-Fungible Tokens
apps.tease: Programmable money, second use: tokens that are unique. Light tour now — a later session goes deep.
apps.description: Provable, transferable ownership of a unique token. The chain records every owner it ever had — the blockchain is the title deed.

examples.name: POAPs
examples.desc: On-chain badges proving you attended an event

examples.name: Property deeds
examples.desc: Propy sold the first house as an NFT

apps.risk: The image usually lives off-chain — "you own the receipt, not the file"
apps.hype: The 2021 picture mania collapsed; the useful part — transferable proof of ownership — remains
apps.stat: $41B traded at the 2021 peak — now utility-focused
apps.later: You'll mint a token of your own and see exactly what is — and isn't — stored on-chain.

visual.bottomLine: One token, one owner, a history nobody can edit.

apps.title: DAOs
apps.subtitle: Decentralised Autonomous Organisations
apps.tease: Programmable money, third use: let a contract run the organisation. Light tour now — a later session goes deep.
apps.description: An organisation run by smart contracts and token votes instead of a board. Proposals are voted on-chain — and the result executes itself.

examples.name: MakerDAO
examples.desc: MKR holders set the rules behind the DAI stablecoin

examples.name: Uniswap DAO
examples.desc: UNI holders steer a multi-billion treasury

examples.name: Gitcoin
examples.desc: Community votes decide which open-source projects get grants

apps.risk: Voter apathy, whale capture, slow in emergencies
apps.hype: "No CEO" sounds great — in practice a few big token holders often decide, and someone still does the work
apps.later: You'll look at a real governance vote and ask who really held the power.

visual.bottomLine: No board, no CEO. Code counts the votes and acts.

smartContract.kickerBody: Everything else in this section — accounts, gas, DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, tokens — is built from this one thing.
smartContract.heading: What is a Smart Contract?
smartContract.lead: A vending machine made of code: insert the coin, the rules fire automatically, and nobody stands between you and the can.

principles.title: Holds its own money
principles.body: The machine keeps the coins. No shopkeeper, no bank account in the middle.

principles.title: Runs exactly as written
principles.body: Same input, same result, every time — for everyone.

principles.title: Nobody can stop or reverse it
principles.body: Once it runs, it ran. Not the owner, not a court, not the author.

business.body: an agreement that enforces itself removes the middleman you used to pay to enforce it.

demo.hint: Insert a coin and watch the rule run itself.

trace.rule: if coin ≥ {{price}} → dispense · otherwise → return coin

demo.undoMsg: There is no undo button. The rule already ran — not the owner, not a bank, not a court can take the can back.
demo.escrowNote: Swap the can for a house deed and the coin for the purchase price — that's escrow without a notary.

smartContract.peek: You'll write and deploy a contract like this one yourself.

tokens.kickerBody: DeFi, NFTs and DAOs all move the same two building blocks around.
tokens.heading: Tokens — The Business Primitive
tokens.lead: A token is a standard-shaped container for value. Because the shape is standard, every wallet, exchange and app already knows how to hold it.

unique.title: Unique — one of a kind
unique.sub: #001 ≠ #002, like a deed or a seat

business.body: issuing a token is cheap and instant. The hard part is the business model and the law around it — not the technology.

tokens.peek: You'll create a token of each kind and see the standard behind it.

useCases.recapBody: Remember the village ledger — every trust problem you saw there shows up again, at industry scale.
useCases.heading: Blockchain Use Cases — Three Patterns, Twelve Industries

groups.tagline: Money, claims, and contracts settle directly between parties — banks, brokers, and clearing houses become optional.

industries.name: Finance & DeFi
industries.hook: Lending, trading, payments — no bank, open 24/7

industries.name: Capital Markets
industries.hook: Tokenised securities settle in seconds, not T+2 days

industries.name: Insurance
industries.hook: Parametric policies auto-pay on verified events

industries.name: CBDCs
industries.hook: Programmable state money — power and peril (see Ethics)

groups.tagline: Anything that needs an unbroken chain of custody gets one — built in, not bolted on.

industries.name: Supply Chain
industries.hook: Track & trace from raw material to consumer

industries.name: Global Trade
industries.hook: Digital letters of credit replace 5-day paper trails

industries.name: Media & Entertainment
industries.hook: Royalties to collaborators on every play, automatically

groups.tagline: People and organisations coordinate without a single platform or registrar in the middle.

industries.name: Digital Identity
industries.hook: You own your credentials, prove age without revealing birthdate

industries.name: Government
industries.hook: Verifiable voting, immutable land registry, transparent procurement

industries.name: Energy & Sustainability
industries.hook: Carbon credits without double-counting, P2P energy trading

industries.name: Law & Real Estate
industries.hook: Escrow + title transfers auto-executed, fractional ownership

useCases.noticeBodyTail: ) shows up across supply chain, healthcare, and media. Industries are different surfaces; the underlying primitive is the same — which is why one platform choice can serve many business cases. A later session picks the platforms apart.

ecosystem.recapBody: Each use case you just saw lives somewhere in this stack — same nodes from §1 at the bottom, same contracts as DeFi/NFTs in the middle, you at the top.
ecosystem.heading: The Blockchain & Web3 Ecosystem
ecosystem.lead: A layered stack — from raw infrastructure at the bottom to end users at the top.

web3.kickerBodyA: Quick historical context: how the web's
web3.kickerTail: has shifted in 30 years — and why Web3 looks different from what came before.
web3.heading: The Evolution of the Internet
web3.lead: Each era defined by what users could do — and who owned the data.

web1.label: Web 1.0
web1.quote: "The internet was a library. You could only look."

web2.label: Web 2.0
bullets: Platforms own and monetize your data
Free services — you are the product
web2.quote: "The internet became interactive. But platforms kept the keys."

web3.label: Web 3.0
web3.quote: "The internet becomes owned by its users. No platform can take it away."

dappComparison.title: Today's App vs dApp
dappComparison.subtitle: Same job for the user — very different plumbing underneath.

items.option2: Smart contracts on a public chain + decentralised storage
You hold your data and assets with your keys
No single point of failure — runs while the network runs

items.option1: Can ban users, delete content, change the terms
items.option2: Nobody can block a transaction once it is on-chain
Token incentives and protocol fees, set by governance

items.option1: Spotify — controls the catalogue, sets the payout
items.option2: Audius — artists upload directly, fans pay in tokens

dappComparison.peek: You'll build a small dApp front-end that talks to your own contract.

ethics.recapTail: that protects the chain from tampering also protects bad rules from being undone. Same property, two faces.
ethics.heading: Ethical Considerations
ethics.lead: Blockchain is not inherently good or bad — its impact depends on how it is designed, governed, and used.
ethics.tensionsLabel: Four tensions to keep in your pocket

themes.title: ⚡ Energy
themes.desc: Bitcoin PoW uses as much power as some countries. Ethereum's PoS cut its footprint by 99.95%.
themes.ask: Is "secure because it's expensive" worth the power bill?

themes.title: 👁️ Surveillance vs Privacy
themes.desc: Public chains are transparent forever — accountability and privacy are in direct tension.
themes.ask: Would you want your bank statement public — forever?

themes.title: 🔒 Irreversibility
themes.desc: "Code is law" has limits. Transactions can't be reversed, even when real people are harmed.
themes.ask: Who do you call when the code is wrong?

themes.title: 🌍 Access & Inclusion
themes.desc: 1.4 billion unbanked adults could access financial services with just a smartphone and a wallet.
themes.ask: A wallet needs a phone, a signal, and a safe seed phrase — who provides those?

ethics.footer: Keep these in mind — the next slide shows the same technology pulled in two opposite directions.

ethicsControl.recapTail: Same technology, two very different answers.
ethicsControl.heading: Blockchain for Good vs Blockchain as Control
ethicsControl.lead: A ledger nobody can quietly alter can protect people from powerful institutions — or hand those institutions a perfect control panel. Design decides which.

good.title: GiveDirectly
good.subtitle: Transparent humanitarian aid
points: Cash sent straight to people in extreme poverty — a mobile wallet, no bank account needed
Every transfer is traceable on-chain: donors can verify the money arrived
Cuts the up-to-30% that traditional aid loses to administration and corruption

good.title: Proof of Humanity
good.subtitle: Identity without institutions
points: Prove you are a real human with a short video + vouching from existing members
No government or company owns the list — nobody can delete you
Enables one-person-one-vote governance and UBI experiments on-chain

control.title: Digital Yuan (e-CNY)
control.subtitle: Programmable money, programmable control
points: Expiry dates and geographic locks — stimulus money that vanishes if unspent
Category bans: alcohol, gambling or donations can be auto-blocked
Any wallet frozen in seconds; every transaction visible to the state by design

control.title: Digital Euro
control.subtitle: Coming soon — questions remain
points: An ECB-issued CBDC, marketed as a modern form of cash
A proposed €3,000 holding cap steers behaviour by design
Unlike cash, every payment is logged — restrictions can be added later, silently

ethicsControl.footerBody: who holds the keys, and who can change the rules? Every system you meet in later sessions gets the same test.

future.title: Future Trends
future.description: The next decade of blockchain will be shaped by convergence with other technologies and solutions to current limitations.

trends.title: 🤖 AI + Blockchain
trends.blurb: Prove what is real — provenance for data and AI outputs.

trends.title: 🔮 Zero-Knowledge Proofs
trends.blurb: Prove a fact without revealing the data behind it.

trends.title: 🔗 Interoperability
trends.blurb: A network of networks — chains that talk to each other.

trends.title: 🪪 Decentralised Identity
trends.blurb: Credentials you own. Prove your age without sharing your birthdate.

trends.title: 🧾 Account Abstraction
trends.blurb: Wallets that feel like normal apps: recovery, sponsored gas.

trends.title: 🏗️ Real-World Assets
trends.blurb: Bonds, property and funds tokenised on-chain — already happening.

future.footerBody: Each of these is a rabbit hole of its own. You now have the vocabulary to follow any of them.

What are the potential challenges to adoption?

quizWeb3.question: What is the fundamental shift that Web3 represents compared to Web2?
options: Faster internet speeds and better streaming quality
Users own their data, identity, and digital assets instead of platforms
Free access to all premium content and services
Government control and regulation of all internet content
quizWeb3.explanation: Web3 shifts ownership from platforms to users through decentralization and cryptographic keys. Instead of companies owning your data, you control your identity and assets via wallets and on-chain protocols.

quizDapp.question: What is a key advantage of a dApp over a traditional centralized application?
options: dApps are always faster and cheaper to use
dApps have no single point of failure — they run as long as the blockchain network exists
dApps don't require an internet connection to function
dApps are always free and generate no revenue
quizDapp.explanation: Because dApps run on decentralized blockchain networks via smart contracts, they have no central server that can fail or be shut down. As long as the underlying blockchain network operates, the dApp continues to function.

quizLayers.question: Which layer of the Web3 ecosystem contains protocols like Ethereum, Solana, and Polygon?
quizLayers.explanation: Ethereum, Solana, and Polygon are L1 blockchains or L2 scaling solutions. They sit between raw infrastructure (nodes, validators, P2P network) and the application protocols (DeFi, NFTs, DAOs) built on top of them.

takeaways.title: Section 3 — Key Takeaways
items: Ethereum turned the blockchain into a programmable world computer — smart contracts, accounts, gas and tokens are the ideas everything else builds on
DeFi, NFTs, and DAOs are what programmable money unlocks: finance, ownership, and organisations without a central operator
The same three patterns — trust without intermediaries, verifiable provenance, self-sovereign coordination — show up across every industry
Web3 = Read + Write + Own: the key shift is that users own their data and digital assets instead of platforms
The technology is neutral: it can deliver aid transparently or build programmable control — design and governance decide which
Bitcoin is one of the simplest blockchains. Everything in this section was a preview — later sessions go deep

knowledgeWall.heading: Knowledge Wall
knowledgeWall.leadA: Every term you've met across Sections 1, 2, and 3 — in one place. Hover any brick to recall its meaning.
knowledgeWall.hoverHint: Hover or tap a brick below to read its definition.

bricks.defn: Distributed Ledger Technology — a database replicated across many independent computers, with no central authority.
A one-way function that turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint. You can't reverse it; tiny input changes flip the output completely.
The specific hash function Bitcoin uses. Always produces 64 hex characters.
Changing one bit of input completely changes the hash output. The "spread" property that makes hashing useful.
Once written into the chain, a record can't be silently altered without leaving evidence everywhere downstream.
Stronger than "tamper-proof": any change breaks visible cryptographic links, so the tampering can't hide.
Replacing trust in people or institutions with trust in math, code, and incentives.
A container of transactions with a header that cryptographically links to the previous block.
The sequence of blocks, each tied to its predecessor through a hash pointer.
The very first block. Has no predecessor — its prev-hash field is conventionally all zeros.
A block's metadata: version, prev hash, merkle root, timestamp, bits (difficulty), and nonce.
A binary tree of hashes. Pairs are hashed together repeatedly until one root remains.
A single hash that summarises every transaction in a block. Change any tx → root changes.
A number a miner cycles through until the block's hash meets the difficulty target.
How many leading zeros the hash must have. Adjusts every 2,016 blocks to keep ~10 min block time.
Approximate time the miner stamped the block. Lives inside the header.
Software that holds your keys. It does NOT hold coins — coins live on-chain. The keys prove the coins are yours.
The one secret that authorises spending. Like a PIN, like a house key. Lose it = lose the funds.
Derived from the private key one-way. Used by others to verify your signatures. Safe to share.
A short hash of the public key. Like an IBAN or a mailbox slot — anyone can send to it.
12 or 24 ordinary English words encoding the master secret. Regenerates the entire wallet on any device.
Cryptographic proof a message was approved by the holder of a specific private key, without revealing the key.
A computer running the blockchain software, storing the chain and validating new transactions/blocks.
Peer-to-peer. No central server — every node talks directly to other nodes.
How thousands of independent nodes agree on the same state of the chain.
Miners spend electricity guessing nonces. Whoever finds a valid hash first wins the right to add a block.
Validators stake tokens as collateral. Misbehave and the stake is slashed. Ethereum switched to PoS in 2022.
Running computers to solve PoW puzzles in exchange for newly minted coins + transaction fees.
If one entity controls majority hash power, they can rewrite recent history. The reason chains want many nodes.
The classic problem: how to reach agreement across a network where some participants may lie or fail.
A split in the chain. Soft fork = backward-compatible; hard fork = creates two incompatible chains.
Trying to send the same coin twice. Consensus + the longest-chain rule prevents it.
The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin. Published the whitepaper Oct 2008, mined the genesis block Jan 2009, vanished 2010.
Bitcoin's 9-page founding document. Surprisingly readable. Linked in the Bibliography.
The absolute maximum number of bitcoins that will ever exist. Hard-coded by every full node.
Every ~4 years the block reward halves. Schedules supply decay; last halving expected around 2140.
Unspent Transaction Output. Bitcoin tracks "unspent coin chunks", not account balances.
Bitcoin's intentionally limited scripting language. Not Turing-complete — no loops, no persistent state.
A Layer-2 network on top of Bitcoin for fast, cheap micropayments. Settles back to L1 periodically.
Simplified Payment Verification. Light clients use Merkle proofs to verify a tx is in a block without storing the chain.
The first programmable blockchain. Launched 2015 by Vitalik Buterin. Where smart contracts became practical.
Ethereum Virtual Machine. The global computer that executes smart contracts identically on every node.
Code stored on a blockchain that runs deterministically when called. The data IS the code IS the rules.
The unit measuring computational work on the EVM. Every operation costs gas; you pay for what you use.
1 gwei = 0.000 000 001 ETH. The unit gas prices are quoted in.
Externally Owned Account. An account controlled by a private key — your Rabby or Zerion wallet is one.
An account controlled by code, not a key. Holds a smart contract's state. Can't initiate transactions on its own.
The 2021 fee market upgrade. Base fee is burned, optional priority tip goes to the validator.
Sept 2022 — Ethereum switched from PoW to PoS. Cut its energy use by 99.95%.
Decentralised application — a frontend talking to smart contracts on-chain instead of a company server.
Decentralised Finance. Lending, trading, derivatives running entirely in smart contracts.
Non-Fungible Token. A unique on-chain asset (ERC-721) with a permanent ownership history.
Decentralised Autonomous Organisation. Governance by smart contract + token votes instead of a board.
The Ethereum standard for fungible tokens (every USDC, every DAI, every LINK).
The Ethereum standard for non-fungible tokens (NFTs).
A token pegged to a stable asset, usually the US dollar. USDC, USDT, DAI.
A service that brings off-chain data on-chain (prices, sports scores, weather). Chainlink is the leading provider.
InterPlanetary File System. Content-addressed decentralised storage often used to host NFT metadata.
A base-layer blockchain (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana). Where consensus + final settlement happens.
A network built on top of an L1 to scale throughput while inheriting its security. Arbitrum, Optimism, Base.
An L2 that batches transactions off-chain and posts a compressed proof back to L1.
Zero-Knowledge Proof. Prove a statement is true without revealing the underlying data.
Wallets that behave like smart contracts: social recovery, gasless txs, session keys. UX upgrade.
Real-World Assets. Tokenising real estate, bonds, commodities on-chain. BlackRock, Franklin Templeton are early.
Central Bank Digital Currency. State-issued digital money — programmable, traceable, sometimes restrictable.
Decentralised Identity. User-controlled digital identity, no central registry to revoke you.

assignment.title: Could a blockchain fix this?
assignment.subtitle: You've seen what blockchains do well — and the course's recurring question: does this problem actually earn a blockchain? Now apply that lens to a real-world problem of your own choosing.
assignment.seedsIntro: Any industry, any scale. Starting points if you're stuck:

steps.label: Form a group, pick one problem

assignment.deliverableIntro: Three parts, in this order. Be concrete and honest — a well-argued "no, a database is enough" scores as well as a yes.

parts.title: Problem statement
parts.desc: Who is affected, what goes wrong today, and why trust or coordination is at the heart of it.

parts.title: Proposed solution
parts.desc: How a blockchain-based approach would work, in plain language. Who runs the network and who uses it?

parts.title: Pros & cons
parts.desc: What a blockchain genuinely adds here — and what it costs. Would a spreadsheet or a trusted middleman do the job?

assignment.footerBody: Creativity gets you a strong problem; critical thinking gets you a strong report. Both are graded.
